database-integration.outcome: Design a booking whose seat record and ticket agree after success, failure or simultaneous requests.
terms: A system for storing and retrieving records reliably.
A unit through which the application works with database records.
A group of changes that succeed or fail together.
A value supplied separately from the command that uses it.

decisions.situation: The last seat is available when two phones request it at the same moment. Both read 1 before either has written.
decisions.action: Reserve using an atomic condition or database lock that lets only one request claim the seat.
decisions.reason: A separate read followed by an unchecked write allows both callers to rely on the same old count.
decisions.check: Run two simultaneous bookings for one remaining seat and verify there is exactly one confirmed ticket.
decisions.tradeoff: Stronger coordination can increase waiting time on a popular route.
decisions.alternative: Rely on disabling the booking button in each phone’s own screen.

decisions.situation: A customer named O’Reilly breaks a booking search assembled by inserting the name directly into a query string.
decisions.action: Bind the name as a query value rather than assembling command text from it.
decisions.reason: Binding keeps the customer’s punctuation inside a value and out of the command structure.
decisions.check: Look up a name with an apostrophe and check that only the matching customer is returned.
decisions.tradeoff: Choosing a dynamic column name requires a separate allowlist rather than ordinary value binding.
decisions.alternative: Strip apostrophes out of all customer names before saving them.

decisions.situation: A ticket insertion fails after availability was reduced, and the bus now shows one fewer available seat with no ticket.
decisions.action: Place both the reduction and ticket insertion inside one transaction.
decisions.reason: A failed second write can then cancel the earlier write instead of leaving contradictory records.
decisions.check: Cause a controlled ticket-insert failure and check that the availability count is unchanged.
decisions.tradeoff: External work such as sending an email is outside a simple database rollback and needs separate handling.
decisions.alternative: Commit the seat reduction first and assume ticket insertion always succeeds.

validation.title: Catch impossible cinema bookings at the door
validation.story: A cinema lets one customer buy 1 through 6 tickets. The app receives a request for 3 tickets to a 7:00 show. Validation means checking supplied information against the rules before using it.
steps: Check its shape. Ticket count must be a whole number, so the word many cannot enter the seat calculation.
Check its allowed range. Three is between 1 and 6. Zero is a number but the cinema does not sell a zero-ticket booking.
Check related facts. All selected seat numbers must belong to that show and the number of selected seats must equal the ticket count.
Only then try to reserve seats that are still available. A valid request can become impossible if someone else reached the seat first.
validation.outcome: Translate a real booking rule into checks a customer can understand and correct.
terms: Checking the kind of value, such as a whole number.
Checking permitted minimum and maximum values.
A condition that depends on more than one supplied value.
An input right at or just beyond a limit.
Information describing which rule an input failed.

decisions.situation: A form limits orders to 6 tickets, but someone sends 60 directly to the server.
decisions.action: Enforce the upper bound at the server before reserving seats.
decisions.reason: An on-screen restriction can be bypassed by a different client.
decisions.check: Send counts 6 and 7 directly and verify only 6 is accepted.
decisions.tradeoff: The client-side check still helps users notice mistakes early.
decisions.alternative: Trust the request because the official form contains a maximum field.

decisions.situation: A request asks for three tickets but lists A1, A1 and A2. The list has three entries.
decisions.action: Check that the selected seats are distinct as well as matching the ticket count.
decisions.reason: Repeating A1 cannot provide two physical seats.
decisions.check: Use A1, A2, A3 as a valid comparison and verify duplicates fail before payment.
decisions.tradeoff: Open-admission events with no assigned seats require a different rule.
decisions.alternative: Approve the order after comparing only the list length with three.

decisions.situation: A train form accepts departure 23:50 and arrival 00:20 the following day. A time-only check rejects it.
decisions.action: Compare full dates and times under an explicit time-zone convention.
decisions.reason: The arrival belongs to the next day and is thirty minutes later despite its smaller clock reading.
decisions.check: Check same-day reversed times, a valid overnight journey and a journey crossing time zones.
decisions.tradeoff: Collecting dates and zones adds fields but removes an otherwise unavoidable ambiguity.
decisions.alternative: Reject every arrival clock time lower than the departure clock time.

exception-handling.title: Explain why a parcel lookup failed
exception-handling.story: Ravi enters parcel P19 and the tracker cannot show its status. The number may be unknown, the input may be malformed, or the storage service may be down. Handling exceptions means responding to these different interruptions deliberately.
steps: If P19 is well formed and a successful search finds no parcel, return the service’s missing-parcel result. The user can recheck the number.
If the storage service times out, say tracking is temporarily unavailable. A failed search is not evidence that the parcel is missing.
Record internal details for staff under a reference such as R4. Show the customer a safe message with that reference rather than passwords or internal file paths.
If the request was changing a parcel record, undo unfinished database changes before returning the error.
exception-handling.outcome: Tell a caller what happened and preserve enough evidence to investigate it.
terms: A signal that ordinary execution could not continue as expected.
Code that decides how to respond to a particular failure.
Giving up on a reply after a set waiting time.
A short number describing the outcome of a web request.
Information staff can use to investigate a failure.

decisions.situation: A parcel search catches a database timeout and tells the customer P19 does not exist.
decisions.action: Return a temporary-service failure and keep the timeout cause for staff.
decisions.reason: The search never completed, so the service has no evidence that P19 is absent.
decisions.check: Simulate an unavailable database and verify the reply differs from a confirmed missing parcel.
decisions.tradeoff: Automatic retry may help reads, but retrying a change can repeat it without safeguards.
decisions.alternative: Treat every lookup exception as a missing record.

decisions.situation: A broken handler sends a customer a full stack trace containing internal folders and a connection string.
decisions.action: Return a short public message with a reference ID and restrict detailed diagnostics to protected logs.
decisions.reason: The customer needs a useful next step while staff need technical details that may reveal secrets.
decisions.check: Trigger a controlled failure and check the user reply omits private values and the reference locates the staff event.
decisions.tradeoff: Protected logs also require redaction, access limits and retention rules.
decisions.alternative: Return the full traceback to make support calls shorter.

decisions.situation: Two callers try to claim parcel P19. One succeeds and the other encounters a known already-claimed condition.
decisions.action: Map the expected conflict to a clear conflict response and leave ownership unchanged.
decisions.reason: A competing claim is a recognized business outcome with a different remedy from a server crash.
decisions.check: Repeat the claim under a second account and verify exactly one owner and an understandable conflict message.
decisions.tradeoff: Access policies may limit how much ownership information the reply can reveal.
decisions.alternative: Catch the conflict as an unknown crash and retry the claim until it succeeds.

logging.title: Trace one missing meal order through a busy kitchen
logging.story: A service handles meal orders 41 and 42 at the same second. Order 42 never reaches the kitchen. A log is a chronological record of events kept for investigation. Times alone cannot separate simultaneous orders.
steps: Give the request for order 42 a reference such as K9. Write an event when the request arrives, another when the order is stored and another when the kitchen receives it. Carry K9 along.
Write named fields for the event, reference and result. This lets someone search for K9 without trying to guess which sentence was used.
Suppose K9 has order_saved followed by kitchen_timeout. A member of staff can now investigate the kitchen connection rather than asking the customer to re-enter payment.
Keep account secrets and personal details out of diagnostic fields. A reference that points to a protected record is often enough.
logging.outcome: Reconstruct one request among many without logging everything the customer sent.
terms: One recorded occurrence, such as an order being saved.
An event written with named fields that can be searched.
A reference shared by events belonging to one request or operation.
An indication of how much attention an event needs.
Removing or hiding sensitive details in a record.

decisions.situation: Events for two orders share the same timestamp. Staff cannot tell which kitchen timeout belongs to order 42.
decisions.action: Propagate one correlation reference through all stages of each individual order.
decisions.reason: Concurrent events can share times, while the reference ties related work together.
decisions.check: Filter records for K9 and confirm only events from the intended request chain appear.
decisions.tradeoff: A reference omitted by a downstream system breaks the chain.
decisions.alternative: Add more timestamp digits and assume they identify related events.

decisions.situation: A login failure logs the full submitted password to help the team reproduce the problem.
decisions.action: Record the failure category and a safe account reference while omitting the password.
decisions.reason: Anyone able to read the logs could otherwise recover the customer’s credential.
decisions.check: Make a test attempt with a distinctive dummy password and confirm it never appears in logs.
decisions.tradeoff: Redacted logs can require a more carefully controlled reproduction for complex failures.
decisions.alternative: Keep the password because failed login attempts can never contain a real password.

decisions.situation: A food shop pages its overnight team for every successful order as well as actual delivery failures.
decisions.action: Assign routine events an informational level and alert on meaningful failure patterns.
decisions.reason: If everything wakes the team, staff may miss a genuine incident among ordinary activity.
decisions.check: Replay successful orders and a sustained failure and verify only the intended condition triggers a page.
decisions.tradeoff: An extremely strict alert can delay detection of an important isolated failure.
decisions.alternative: Turn all logging off to stop the overnight pages.

api-testing.title: Check a reservation without selling a real ticket
api-testing.story: A museum charges 50 rupees for a standard ticket and accepts up to four tickets per request. A developer wants to change the booking service and know quickly if an ordinary family visit still works. A test supplies a known situation and checks an observable result.
steps: First check the price calculation by itself. With a price of 50 and quantity 3, the result should be 150. A small check of one piece of logic is a unit test.
Next send a test booking through the same web address and field names the app uses. Verify the success status, quantity 3, total 150 and one saved booking. This checks more than the calculation.
Start each test with known museum seats in a test database. This prepared starting data is called a fixture. Avoid touching real bookings.
Try a quantity of five. The expected result is a clear rejection and zero bookings saved. Checking what stayed unchanged is part of testing a failure.
api-testing.outcome: Choose a small test for arithmetic and a service-level test for the actual customer workflow.
terms: A check that the observed result matches an expectation.
Known data or resources set up for a test.
A focused check of one small piece of behavior.
A check that calls the service through its public request and response interface.
The agreed inputs, outputs and outcomes callers rely on.

decisions.situation: A test checks only that the booking endpoint returns 200. A bug returns a successful-looking message with total 15 instead of 150.
decisions.action: Assert the expected quantity, total and stored booking as well as the agreed success status.
decisions.reason: A status alone does not verify the content or side effects the client needs.
decisions.check: Introduce a deliberately wrong total in a disposable run and confirm the test fails.
decisions.tradeoff: Checking every unimportant display field can make tests fragile during harmless changes.
decisions.alternative: Add more repetitions of the status-only assertion.

decisions.situation: A rejection test passes alone but fails after a previous test fills the museum’s last seat.
decisions.action: Give each test isolated seat data and clean up changes deterministically.
decisions.reason: The starting seat count otherwise depends on which test ran first.
decisions.check: Run the tests in both orders and independently and compare the outcomes.
decisions.tradeoff: Creating fresh data costs setup time for large test suites.
decisions.alternative: Require everyone to run the tests in one permanent order.

decisions.situation: A payment service is slow and charges real cards. A test needs to verify what the museum does after a declined payment.
decisions.action: Supply a controlled test payment provider that reports a decline and inspect the booking state.
decisions.reason: A predictable decline exercises the museum’s failure handling without creating real charges.
decisions.check: Verify the failure response and that no ticket was confirmed for the declined payment.
decisions.tradeoff: A test substitute does not verify the real provider’s exact protocol, which needs a separate integration check.
decisions.alternative: Use a real customer’s card and hope this payment is declined.

backend-security.title: Protect the school’s report download
backend-security.story: A school lets each family download its own report. The screen asks for a report ID, such as R12. The server must decide which file that signed-in family can receive and what information belongs in the reply. A curious person can alter anything their browser sends.
steps: Treat the supplied R12 as a request, not proof of permission. Look up the report and verify the signed-in family is allowed to receive it.
Choose the stored file using the school’s own mapping. A caller-supplied path such as ../private should never be used to wander outside the permitted directory.
Run the download service with access only to the reports it needs. If something fails, narrower permissions limit the damage.
Return only the fields intended for parents. Check the actual response for staff notes even if the screen does not display them.
backend-security.outcome: Identify the caller-controlled pieces of a request and enforce independent checks at the service.
terms: A point where information arrives from someone or something with different permissions.
Giving a program only the access it needs for its job.
An explicit set of permitted values or actions.
Sending or keeping only the information needed for the task.
Checking whether a caller may act on a particular protected item.

decisions.situation: A school report endpoint accepts a filename. Someone submits a path that goes up one directory and points to a private staff file.
decisions.action: Look up an approved report ID, and enforce containment inside the allowed report directory before opening a file.
decisions.reason: File path syntax can navigate outside the intended folder even when the request came through a normal web form.
decisions.check: Test an allowed report plus an attempted parent-directory path and verify no outside file contents are returned.
decisions.tradeoff: If uploads may contain symbolic links, containment must account for where they resolve.
decisions.alternative: Check only that the text ends with .pdf before opening the requested path.

decisions.situation: A report page hides teachers’ private notes, but the network reply still contains those notes in an unused field.
decisions.action: Construct the server response from an explicit set of fields intended for the family.
decisions.reason: A caller can read the raw reply regardless of what the page chooses to draw.
decisions.check: Inspect the response body as a parent and verify private notes are absent.
decisions.tradeoff: A staff workflow needing the notes requires a separate authorized response.
decisions.alternative: Hide the note more thoroughly with page styling.

decisions.situation: A read-only timetable service can edit all student grades with its database credentials.
decisions.action: Give its database account read access only to the schedule data it needs.
decisions.reason: A compromised timetable service can cause only changes allowed by its underlying permissions.
decisions.check: Using the service account, confirm permitted schedule reads succeed and grade updates are rejected.
decisions.tradeoff: New legitimate capabilities may require carefully reviewed permission changes.
decisions.alternative: Keep broad permissions and rely on a rule telling future developers not to edit grades.
